content: 1. Fortification of staple foods, when implemented correctly, is an effective, straightforward, and cost-efficient strategy to provide additional vitamins and minerals to large segments of the population. 2. Rice is widely cultivated across the globe due to its adaptability to diverse climates. 3. Industrial fortification of rice with vitamins and minerals has been practiced for many years in several countries within the WHO Eastern Mediterranean Region, Western Pacific Region, and Region of the Americas, where rice is a staple food regularly used in the preparation of many local dishes. 4. Decisions regarding the types and amounts of nutrients to add to fortified rice are typically based on the nutritional needs and dietary gaps of the target populations, the usual level of rice consumption, the sensory and physical effects of the fortificant on rice kernels, the fortification processing methods, the availability and coverage of fortification of other staple foods, the population's use of vitamin and mineral supplements, costs, feasibility of implementation, and consumer acceptability. 5. Rice kernels can be fortified with various micronutrients, such as iron, folic acid, other B-complex vitamins, vitamin A, and zinc. Some of these nutrients are used to restore intrinsic nutritional content lost during milling, while others are added for fortification purposes. 6. The bioavailability of these nutrients depends significantly on the processing methods used in the production of fortified kernels. 7. The purpose of this guideline is to provide global, evidence-based recommendations on fortifying rice with micronutrients as a strategy to improve the health status of populations. 8. The guideline aims to assist Member States and their partners in making informed decisions about appropriate nutrition actions to achieve the 2030 Sustainable Development Goals and the global targets outlined in the Comprehensive Implementation Plan on Maternal, Infant, and Young Child Nutrition. 9. The recommendations in this guideline are intended for policymakers, their expert advisors, and technical and program staff in ministries and organizations involved in designing, implementing, and scaling up nutrition actions for public health. 10. This guideline complements the WHO/FAO Guidelines on Food Fortification with Micronutrients and the Pan American Health Organization document on iron compounds for food fortification in Latin America and the Caribbean. 11. A WHO guideline is any document containing WHO recommendations about health interventions, whether clinical, public health, or policy-related. 12. A recommendation provides guidance on what policymakers, healthcare providers, or patients should do, implying a choice between different interventions that impact health and resource use. 13. All WHO guidelines are approved by the WHO Guidelines Review Committee. 14. B-complex vitamins include thiamine (B1), riboflavin (B2), niacin (B3), pyridoxine (B6), folate (B9), and cyanocobalamin (B12). Thiamine, riboflavin, niacin, and folic acid are commonly referred to by name, while the others are referred to by their vitamin numbers. 15. Fortification of rice with iron is recommended as a public health strategy to improve the iron status of populations in settings where rice is a staple food (strong recommendation, moderate-certainty evidence). 16. Fortification of rice with vitamin A may be used as a public health strategy to improve both iron and vitamin A nutrition in populations (conditional recommendation, low-certainty evidence). 17. Fortification of rice with folic acid may be used as a public health strategy to improve folate nutritional status in populations (conditional recommendation, very low-certainty evidence). 18. The number and amounts of nutrients added to fortified rice should be adapted to the specific needs of each country. 19. If other staple foods (e.g., wheat flour, maize flour, or cornmeal) and micronutrient interventions are implemented effectively, the suggested fortification levels for rice may need to be adjusted downward. 20. A combined fortification strategy using multiple food vehicles appears to be an effective option for reaching all segments of the population. 21. Several methods are available for fortifying rice, and the choice of method depends on local technology, costs, and preferences. 22. The process of adding nutrients to rice through dusting reduces the number of nutrients consumed in settings where rice is commonly washed before cooking. 23. Washing and cooking practices among a population are important considerations when selecting a method for rice fortification. For example, rinse-resistant methods are essential to ensure nutrient retention if rice is commonly washed before cooking. 24. Rice milling results in the loss of a significant proportion of B vitamins and minerals, which are predominantly found in the outer germ and bran layers. 25. Nutrient losses during milling can be minimized through parboiling, a process in which raw rice is soaked in water, partially steamed, and then dried and milled, causing some B vitamins to migrate further into the grain. 26. Since some of the fatand micronutrient-rich bran layers are removed during rice milling, restoring thiamine, niacin, and riboflavin in the fortification profile should remain a regular practice. 27. The prevalence of vitamin B12 depletion and deficiency is high across all age groups, reaching up to 50% in some countries. 28. Including vitamin B12 in fortified staples is recommended when folic acid is also added to avoid the masking effect of folic acid on vitamin B12 deficiency. 29. Fortification of rice with iron has been challenging because most bioavailable iron powders used in food fortification are colored, altering the appearance of fortified kernels compared to unfortified ones. 30. Ferric pyrophosphate is often chosen for rice fortification because it is a white powder, although its bioavailability is low. 31. Human absorption studies have shown that adding enhancing compounds, such as citric acid or trisodium citrate mixtures, can increase iron absorption from ferric pyrophosphate. 32. Mandatory rice-fortification programs can only be effective if they are properly implemented and legislation is enforced. 33. Food fortification should be guided by national standards, with quality-assurance and quality-control systems in place to ensure high-quality fortification. 34. Continuous program monitoring should be conducted to ensure high-quality implementation, including monitoring consumption patterns and evaluating micronutrient status in the population to adjust fortification levels over time. 35. National-scale rice fortification requires a large, cost-effective, and sustainable supply of fortified kernels. 36. In malaria-endemic areas, providing iron through rice fortification as a public health strategy should be done alongside measures to prevent, diagnose, and treat malaria. 37. Behavior-change communication strategies may be necessary to overcome barriers and create and maintain demand for fortified rice. 38. Research priorities include studying the bioavailability of different iron compounds for food fortification, the effects of phytate content on iron absorption, and the efficacy and effectiveness of rice fortification with nutrients other than iron in various settings and population groups.
